title: RAG, hybrid search and reranking
scenario: Long technical explanation of a retrieval pipeline (BM25 + embeddings → RRF fusion → cross-encoder reranking → generation) with a protected formula, measured trade-offs, and hedged claims whose conditions and limits must stay with them.
audience: Engineers building or tuning a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system
objective: Understand what each retrieval stage contributes, how the stages connect, what each costs, and under which conditions each helps — without turning 'can improve' into 'always improves'.

sourceFiles.title: Hybrid search and reranking in the Harbor assistant

units.quote: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers a question in two stages: it first retrieves passages from a document collection, then asks a language model to write an answer from those passages.
The model never sees the rest of the collection, so the answer can only be as good as the passages that retrieval hands it.

critical.note: The bound that motivates the whole design: generation can't exceed retrieval.

units.quote: This note describes the retrieval design of the Harbor support assistant, an internal tool that answers questions over about 40,000 help-centre articles and release notes.

omittable.note: Says what the note is about; the collection size is not used by any claim.

units.quote: Keyword retrieval scores a passage by the query terms it contains, weighted so that rare terms count for more than common ones.
BM25 is the usual scoring function for this; it also dampens the effect of a term repeated many times and corrects for passage length.
BM25 needs no training and is cheap to run, which is why it remains the baseline.
Its strength is exact matching.
A query for the error code `E-4012` or the setting `sync.retry_window` finds the passages that contain those strings, even when they appear only once in the whole collection.
Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch: a user who asks "why does my upload stall" will not match a passage that only says "transfers pause when the connection drops".

critical.note: BM25's weakness; it is the reason a second signal is worth adding.

units.quote: Vector retrieval turns the query and every passage into embeddings, lists of numbers produced by an encoder model, and returns the passages whose embeddings lie closest to the query's.
Passages that mean the same thing end up close together even when they share no words, so the stalled-upload question can find the passage about paused transfers.
Embeddings are weaker on exact codes and identifiers.

critical.note: Vector retrieval's weakness; the complement of BM25's strength.

units.quote: To the encoder, `E-4012` and `E-4021` look almost the same, and a rare product name may be split into fragments that carry little meaning.
In our tests, vector retrieval alone missed the correct passage for 31 of 50 queries that consisted mainly of an error code.
Embeddings must also be recomputed whenever the encoder changes, which for this collection takes about 6 hours.
Hybrid search runs both retrievers on the same query and merges their result lists.
Hybrid search can improve recall when lexical and semantic signals are complementary, that is, when each retriever finds relevant passages that the other misses.

critical.note: A possibility under a condition: 'can improve … when … complementary'. Neither the hedge nor the condition may be dropped.

units.quote: If both retrievers tend to return the same passages, or if one of them is poorly tuned for the collection, merging adds latency without adding much.

critical.note: When the condition fails, hybrid search costs latency for little gain.

units.quote: BM25 scores and vector similarities sit on different scales, so they cannot simply be added together.
We use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which ignores the raw scores and uses only the rank of each passage in each list.
A passage receives `1/(k + rank)` from every list it appears in, and the contributions are summed.

critical.note: The fusion formula must survive exactly.

units.quote: We set `k = 60`, a common default; a larger k flattens the difference between the top ranks and the lower ones.

critical.note: The constant's value is part of the formula.

units.quote: Each retriever returns its top 50 passages, so the fused list holds at most 100 candidates, and usually fewer because some passages appear in both lists.
This stage is tuned for recall rather than precision: the goal is to make sure the right passage is somewhere in the list, not that it comes first.
Raising the limit to 100 per retriever put the right passage in the list slightly more often, but it roughly doubled the time spent reranking, so we kept 50.
A reranker then rescores the fused candidates.
We use a cross-encoder, a model that reads the query and one passage together and outputs a single relevance score.
Because it sees both texts at once, it judges relevance far more accurately than either retriever.
That accuracy is expensive, so the cross-encoder runs only on the fused candidates, never on the whole collection.
After reranking we keep the top 8 passages.
Reranking improves the precision of the top results, but it does not guarantee that the final answer is correct.

critical.note: Precision of the ranking is not correctness of the answer.

units.quote: The reranker can only reorder what retrieval found: if the right passage is not among the candidates, reranking cannot recover it.

critical.note: The reranker can't add a passage retrieval missed.

units.quote: A passage can also be highly relevant and still out of date, which no relevance score will detect.
The language model receives the question and the top 8 passages, and is instructed to answer only from them and to cite the passages it used.
If none of the passages addresses the question, it should say so rather than answer from its general knowledge.

critical.note: The fallback when retrieval found nothing useful.

units.quote: Citations let a reader check each claim against its passage, but they do not show whether the passage itself is current.

For example, asked "What does E-4012 mean?", the assistant retrieves the error-code table through BM25 and the article on resumable uploads through vector search, and the reranker keeps both in the top 8, so the answer can define the code and explain the fix.
Every stage buys relevance with time or money.
On an internal test set of 400 questions, we measured:

| Configuration | Correct passage in top 8 | Median latency | Cost per 1,000 queries |
|---|---|---|---|
| BM25 only | 61% | 35 ms | $0.02 |
| Vector only | 68% | 60 ms | $0.10 |
| Hybrid (RRF) | 79% | 70 ms | $0.12 |
| Hybrid + reranker | 88% | 190 ms | $0.95 |
Reranking adds about 120 ms per query, most of it spent running the cross-encoder over up to 100 candidates, and it accounts for most of the cost increase.
These figures come from one collection and one query set; a collection with fewer exact identifiers may see a smaller gain from BM25, and a different reranker will have a different latency.

critical.note: The measurements don't generalise as they stand.

units.quote: Teams with a strict latency budget can rerank fewer candidates, for example the top 30 of the fused list instead of all of them, at some cost in recall.
Hybrid search widens the net, reranking sorts the catch, and generation can only work with the passages it is given.
Each step helps only under its own conditions, and none of them makes the final answer certain to be right.

critical.note: The takeaway, which carries its own limit.

safeToOmit.why: Framing sentence naming the system and collection; nothing else depends on it.

The Harbor assistant, its collection size, error codes, setting names and every measured figure (31 of 50, 400 questions, the table, 120 ms, 6 hours) are invented.
